reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes BitClub Network investment packages by citing earnings and returns and presenting package purchases as a route to lifetime income. The speaker calls a $500 entry accessible, tells viewers to invest, and includes an instruction to register through the link below the video. The material does not verify the claimed figures or establish the registration destination or payment process.

citations.quote: once I've purchased a package in Bit Club Network, I will finally get a lifetime income from the Bit Club Network while it will work
Please note there are three pools. Pools №1, 2, 3. This one is worth $500, this one is $1000, and this one is $2000.
the pools for 2000 they are more profitable than for 1000 and a pool plus a thousand is more profitable than for five hundred

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker qualifies the most expansive income claim: it lasts only "while it will work," not unconditionally. He also describes his projection as "my hypothetical guess" and acknowledges a difficult period for Bitcoin. Those qualifications matter when deciding whether this is a guaranteed-return pitch or an investor discussing uncertain results. The figures may be optimistic, but the speaker does not present every future outcome as settled.

citations.quote: I will finally get a lifetime income from the Bit Club Network while it will work
my hypothetical guess
the company has survived the difficult situation of Bitcoin last summer

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited pool prices identify what the speaker is discussing; they do not by themselves establish a guaranteed payout. His comparison of pool profitability is expressly drawn from experience, not a complete set of terms offered to every viewer. Even the lifetime-income phrase ends with a condition the opening omits: "while it will work." The registration overlay is promotional, but it does not erase that qualification.

citations.quote: out of my experience I want to tell you that it works
while it will work

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A conditional phrase is not a meaningful risk explanation when the same sentence says buying a package will produce lifetime income. The speaker also describes buying once and receiving money continuously, while the video directs viewers to register. Calling one projection hypothetical does not change the purchase-and-return message.

citations.quote: once I've purchased a package in Bit Club Network, I will finally get a lifetime income from the Bit Club Network while it will work
when you buy once and get free constantly get money

opening.argument: Judge, much of this presentation is a walk-through of an account and its calculations. The speaker dates his own account, asks viewers to calculate alongside him, and then turns to the three pools and reinvestment settings. The displayed account page lets viewers inspect shares, paid amounts, and re-purchase percentages. That is evidence of an operational demonstration, even if the presenter also expresses enthusiasm. An illustrated personal result is not, without more, proof that every viewer is promised the same result.

citations.quote: here is my business account, from which you could identify my investment. I opened it on the 19th of November 2014.
let's calculate together
Please note there are three pools. Pools №1, 2, 3.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats the calculation and pool comparison as solicitation simply because money is involved. But the speaker explicitly returns to a "calculation of passive income" and proposes looking at another account's returns. The registration instruction supports a promotional reading, yet it does not make the account demonstration imaginary or establish that the displayed amounts are a promised outcome for viewers.

citations.quote: Back to calculation of passive income. Let's look.
The next step is to log in to the new account built from February and see the new returns there

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The demonstration is the vehicle for the pitch. The speaker converts claimed account results into a daily dollar figure, compares paid packages by profitability, and says a purchased package can generate lifetime income. The visible registration instruction gives viewers a next step. Showing an account does not independently verify its returns or turn the purchase claim into a neutral tutorial.

once I've purchased a package in Bit Club Network, I will finally get a lifetime income from the Bit Club Network while it will work

opening.argument: Judge, the visible offer can be read as priced participation in mining pools, not a demonstrated theft mechanism. The speaker identifies three pool prices, while the account display shows shares, payments, and re-purchase settings. The presentation invites registration, but these materials do not show a viewer making a deposit, surrendering credentials, or receiving a guaranteed payout. The prosecution's strongest evidence establishes promotion of a paid activity; it does not establish what happens to a viewer after registration.

citations.quote: Please note there are three pools. Pools №1, 2, 3. This one is worth $500, this one is $1000, and this one is $2000.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution is right that the presenter links packages with returns. But the prices alone are participation amounts, and the cited account screen presents mining-pool shares and re-purchase information. A registration prompt does not show the destination's payment process or prove that the displayed business activity is fictitious. The conclusion asks the judge to infer a mechanism the video does not reveal.

citations.quote: This one is worth $500, this one is $1000, and this one is $2000.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The issue is the pitch shown here, not whether a later payment can be observed. The speaker links buying a package to ongoing income, calls the $500 entry accessible, and the video directs viewers to register. An account interface displaying shares and payments does not verify mining proceeds or establish that the promoted returns are sound.
